messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Film Director
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Distraction: I distract myself with something else
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas, a 52‑year‑old European film director, remembers the night the world narrowed to a single, dark cabin on a rain‑slick highway. The car he had driven to a remote shoot site skidded off the road, the engine sputtered, and he was thrown into a silent, oppressive darkness that lasted for what felt like an eternity. The image of his own reflected eyes in the cracked glass, the muffled thud of the impact, the scent of wet earth—these pictures replay in his mind with brutal clarity, a vivid memory that never fades. Thomas thinks about why this terrible event happened to him, the way his mind has begun to ask, “Why me?” that question haunts him, fueling an appraisal that he feels inadequate, a bad cop, and that he has become unrecognisable. Those negative appraisals do more than sit in his thoughts; they push him to adopt a handful of maladaptive strategies: he now shuns any circumstance that reminds him of the accident, particularly darkness; he seeks meaning in every possible explanation, often sitting alone for hours trying to piece together why fate had chosen him; and he distracts himself with the meticulous planning of his next shoot, turning his creative mind into a shield. The constant threat that hangs over Thomas is palpable. An unexpected creak of the set’s rigging or the sudden clang of a camera tripod is enough to set his heart racing; he feels a high alert when any sound seems too loud or too sudden. Because of the relentless hypervigilance and the startle response that catches him off guard at ordinary noises, he is on guard all the time, a state that fuels and is fueled by his fear of darkness and loud sounds. This threat compels him to avoid the very situations that might restore him to the world he once knew. The avoidance becomes a strategy, a way to keep the terror at bay. The more he relies on these avoidance habits, the deeper the threat feels, a loop that tightens with each missed opportunity to confront the past. In the days that followed the crash, Thomas would skip night shoots, leave the studio early, and whenever a bright flash of a flashbulb or a sudden hiss of a camera’s shutter startled him, he would instinctively flee the scene, his sense of safety continually on a precipice. Thomas’s memories of that night, the vivid images of the car’s broken side, the smell of burnt plastic, the cold of the cabin’s interior, feed back into his perception of threat. The clarity of these memories means that a sudden noise—a clatter from the crew’s equipment or a siren in the distance—can instantly conjure that night’s terror. The same vivid images also deepen his negative appraisals. He is convinced that the world is now a dangerous place that rewards him with peril rather than purpose, and this conviction hardens his sense of inadequacy. As his maladaptive strategies intensify—his avoidance of dark environments, his relentless search for meaning, his constant mental redirection—his memories become more intrusive, and he finds himself revisiting that cabin in his mind at random, the images sharpening each time. His strategies of avoidance and distraction, in turn, reinforce his negative self‑view; he feels as if he cannot cope, that he has failed both as a director and as a person. The cycle that binds his memory to his threat, his threat to his maladaptive strategies, and his maladaptive strategies back to his memory and negative appraisals has tightened with every sleepless night and every skipped meeting with his partner. The film set is where Thomas’s avoidance becomes most evident. He refuses to work on projects that require night shoots, fearing the black darkness that once trapped him. When the crew’s director of photography begins a sudden test of a new strobe light, Thomas’s heart races; the bright flash triggers the same vivid image of the cabin’s glass, and he stumbles out of the control room, leaving a crucial scene unfinished. His partner, who has watched his anxiety grow, often offers gentle reminders that the darkness on the set is merely artificial and controllable, but Thomas feels that his mind cannot separate reality from the nightmare. The repeated avoidance has begun to strain his relationship; he feels increasingly distant, as if he is retreating into a self‑constructed barrier to keep the pain at bay. Now, after months of sleepless nights, of frantic workdays punctuated by the abrupt startle of a clack, Thomas finally seeks help. What has pushed him to this point is the relentless erosion of his creative confidence and the growing sense that his identity as a film director—his life’s work—is slipping away. He fears that his avoidance will become a permanent wall that isolates him from the very stories he wants to tell. At the same time, he hopes to reclaim the ability to navigate a world that no longer feels like a constant threat, to stand on a set without the heart racing at a simple echo of a camera shutter. In the quiet moments between meetings, Thomas clutches the memory of that dark cabin, aware that he is caught in a loop that has left him feeling inadequate and unrecognisable, but he also yearns for the day when the lights on set will no longer flash like a warning sign but simply illuminate a new scene.
